content: The studies evaluated the relationship between the exposure status of participants and their health outcomes. However, due to the potential for bias in the assessment of exposure and outcomes, these studies were rated as having a medium to high risk of bias in this domain. Despite this, the sample size at the final time point remained robust, with over 1,000 participants, leading to a classification of low to medium risk of bias for this study in this domain. Statistical analysis for one study was rated as low risk of bias, while four other studies, including the first study, were rated as high risk of bias due to uncontrolled data. Six studies were included in the review, reporting on outcomes such as wasting, underweight, stunting, linear growth, height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), iron status, anemia, and changes in fruit and vegetable (FV) intake over time. All six studies examined the association between varying frequencies of FV or nutrient-poor snack (NPS) consumption. However, none of the studies investigated the impact of differing varieties or amounts of FV or NPS on dietary and health outcomes. One study from Indonesia (Ahmad, 2018) found no association between the frequency of consuming green leafy and orange vegetables and wasting, underweight, or stunting in children aged 6–23 months. Similarly, no significant relationship was observed between vegetable consumption frequency and very low iron stores (ferritin <15 μg/L). Another study from Brazil (Silva, 2007) found no association between the consumption of dark green vegetables and anemia prevalence in children aged 6–12 months. For fruit consumption, Ahmad (2018) reported no association between the frequency of fruit consumption and wasting, underweight, or stunting in children aged 6–23 months. However, a trend suggested lower HAZ scores with less frequent fruit consumption, though findings were inconsistent. Daily fruit consumption was significantly associated with lower anemia prevalence compared to less frequent consumption, as shown in a study adjusted for family income and iron supplement use. Regarding legumes and beans, Ahmad (2018) found no association between legume consumption frequency and wasting, underweight, or stunting in children aged 6–23 months. Similarly, Silva (2007) reported no significant association between bean consumption and anemia prevalence in children aged 6–12 months. A study from China (Chang, 2007) found that less frequent consumption of both vegetables and fruits was associated with higher stunting and underweight prevalence in children aged 6–24 months. This study also reported a trend of lower HAZ scores among children consuming FV less frequently. For longitudinal data, Bjelland (2013) examined changes in vegetable and fruit consumption from 18 months to 7 years of age in Norway. The study found that most children either decreased or remained stable in their consumption patterns, with only a small percentage increasing their intake. For example, 74% of boys decreased their vegetable consumption from high (>7 times/week) to lower levels between 18 and 36 months, while 26% remained stable. In summary, the review aimed to assess the effects of varying frequencies and types of FV and NPS consumption on dietary and health outcomes. However, the available data did not allow for causal conclusions. The six included studies, five of which were cross-sectional and one longitudinal, reported heterogeneous outcomes and consumption frequencies. Outcomes included wasting, underweight, stunting, linear growth, HAZ, iron status, anemia, and changes in FV intake over time. For vegetable consumption, three studies did not specify the types of vegetables consumed.
